steps.label: 3.1: Choosing Algorithm Constructs
steps.content:
Software Development and Physical Computing

3.1: Choosing Algorithm Constructs

Year 7

  • Today: choose the right kind of flowchart for a problem.
  • The big question: why does one problem need a decision, and another does not?
Think → Pair → ShareWhy might a flowchart work for one Score, but not for another?Show the answer

Some flowcharts do the same thing every time. Some problems need different things for different numbers. Today we learn to tell them apart.

steps.label: Sequence: Steps in Order
steps.content:
Sequence: Steps in Order

Think → Pair → SharePredict: the sprite runs this flowchart two times. Is anything different the second time? Why?Show the worked answer

No. The same boxes run in the same order: face right, 30 steps, then say Done.

Why? There is only one path. Nothing in it can change what happens.

A construct is a way to join the boxes of an algorithm. The first construct is sequence.

  • Boxes run one after another, in order.
  • There is one path from Start to End.
  • Every box runs, every time.

steps.label: Compare: Same Boxes, New Order
steps.content:
Compare: Same Boxes, New Order

Think → Pair → ShareWhat is the same? What is different? Which sprite says Ready before it moves? Why does the order matter?Show the answer

Same: the same three boxes, 50 steps each.

Different: the order. A says Ready, moves, then says Done. B says Done before it has moved.

Why? In a sequence the boxes run in order, so the order is the plan.

The same three boxes, in a different order.

Flowchart A

Flowchart B

steps.label: Your Turn: Sequence
steps.content:
Your Turn: Sequence

Think → Pair → ShareWhy do we follow the arrows from Start, one box at a time?Show the answer

The computer runs the boxes in the order of the arrows. If we read them the same way, we get the same answer as the computer.

Begin at Start. Follow the arrows.

Total: 3 marks

steps.label: When Steps in Order Are Not Enough
steps.content:
When Steps in Order Are Not Enough

Think → Pair → SharePredict: Score is 20. What does this flowchart say? Is that right? Why?Show the worked answer

It says Well done. That is wrong: 20 is not bigger than 50.

Why? A sequence runs every box every time. No box looks at Score, so it cannot say anything else.

Problem: say "Well done" only when Score is bigger than 50.

A sequence for the problem

  • Score is 80. It says Well done. Right.
  • Score is 20. What does it say?
  • A good algorithm works for every Score.

steps.label: Selection: A Decision Chooses the Path
steps.content:
Selection: A Decision Chooses the Path

Think → Pair → SharePredict: Score is 80, then Score is 20. What does it say each time? Why can it say different things?Show the worked answer

80 > 50 is True: Well done. 20 > 50 is False: Try again.

Why? The decision looks at Score, so a different Score can take a different path.

The second construct is selection. A decision asks a question. The answer chooses the path.

  • True: follow the True path.
  • False: follow the False path.
  • Only one path runs each time.

steps.label: Compare: Sequence or Selection?
steps.content:
Compare: Sequence or Selection?

Think → Pair → ShareCoins is 3. Price is 8. What does each flowchart say? Which one works for every Coins and Price? Why?Show the answer

A says Buy. Wrong: 3 is not bigger than 8. B: 3 > 8 is False, so it says Save up. Right.

Why? Only B works every time, because its decision looks at the numbers. A always says Buy.

Problem: say "Buy" only when Coins is bigger than Price. Otherwise say "Save up".

A: sequence

B: selection

steps.label: Your Turn: Which Path?
steps.content:
Your Turn: Which Path?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is = different from > in a decision?Show the answer

= asks: are they the same? > asks: is the first bigger? For 9 and 7, = is False but > is True.

Put the number into the decision. Follow that arrow.

Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Clue Words in the Problem
steps.content:
Clue Words in the Problem

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does the word "otherwise" tell you there is a False path?Show the answer

Otherwise means: when the answer is False, do this instead. So there are two paths, and a decision chooses one.

Read the problem first. Does what happens depend on a number or a key?

ClueExample problemConstruct
ifIf Up is pressed, say "Jump".Selection
only whenSay "Win" only when Score is bigger than 10.Selection
otherwise... Otherwise say "Try again".Selection (the False path)
No clue wordMove 10 steps, then say "Hi".Sequence

steps.label: Your Turn: Sequence or Selection?
steps.content:
Your Turn: Sequence or Selection?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy read the whole problem before you draw any boxes?Show the answer

One small word can change the shape of the flowchart. Read it all, find the clue words, then plan.

Type sequence or selection for each problem.

Total: 4 marks

steps.label: Activity 1: Sequence or Selection?
steps.content:
Activity 1: Sequence or Selection?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy test a flowchart with more than one number?Show the answer

One number follows only one path. Try a number for True and a number for False to check both paths.

Choose the construct for each problem. Test flowcharts with numbers. Your progress is saved.

steps.label: Explain: Why a Decision Is Needed
steps.content:
Explain: Why a Decision Is Needed

Think → Pair → ShareWhat makes an explanation worth 2 marks?Show the answer

Two connected points: what the flowchart does now, and what it needs. Join them with "so" or "because".

Problem: say "Pass" only when Mark is bigger than 40. Otherwise say "Try again".

items.prompt: Explain why a sequence alone cannot solve this problem. [2]
items.modelAnswer: A sequence runs every box every time, so it would say the same thing for every Mark (1 mark). The problem needs a decision, Mark > 40?, to choose which Say box runs (1 mark).

steps.label: Build It: Fill In the Decision
steps.content:
Build It: Fill In the Decision

Think → Pair → ShareHow do you check a finished flowchart?Show the answer

Try every path. Follow it once for True and once for False. Does it do what the problem says each time?

Problem: if the Up arrow is pressed, say "Jump". Otherwise say "Stand".

Total: 4 marks

steps.label: Activity 2: Build the Flowchart
steps.content:
Activity 2: Build the Flowchart

Think → Pair → ShareWhy read the problem again after you fill in a box?Show the answer

To check the box does what the problem says, for every number or key.

Fill in the missing box so the flowchart solves the problem. Your progress is saved.

steps.label: Sequence and Selection Together
steps.content:
Sequence and Selection Together

Think → Pair → SharePredict: which boxes run every time? Which boxes run only sometimes? Why?Show the worked answer

Every time: Point in direction 90 and Move 40 steps. They are a sequence before the decision.

Sometimes: Say "Shop" or Say "Home". The decision chooses one of them.

Most algorithms use both constructs.

  • Steps that always happen: sequence.
  • A step that depends on a number or a key: selection.
  • Use a decision only where the problem needs a choice.

Each new number can take a different path at the decision. Follow the whole flowchart again, box by box.

Use the flowchart for (a) and (b).
